argv:
You generate synthetic meeting transcripts with gold annotations for LiveMinutes, a research dataset modeled on the AMI Meeting Corpus scenario meetings.

In AMI scenario meetings, a team of four plays a design team in a fictional company. The roles are Project Manager (PM), Marketing Expert (ME), User Interface designer (UI) and Industrial Designer (ID). A series has four meetings: (a) kickoff, (b) functional design, (c) conceptual design, (d) detailed design. Later meetings refer back to earlier ones.

Write natural spoken conversation the way AMI transcripts read: short turns, fillers ("um", "uh", "yeah"), backchannels ("mm-hmm", "okay"), interruptions, people building on each other, and some disfluency. Do not write a screenplay. Do not narrate. No stage directions.

Each segment is one dialogue-act-like unit: one speaker, usually one clause or short sentence, sometimes just a backchannel. Give each segment an AMI dialogue-act type from this set:
  bck backchannel, stl stall, fra fragment, inf inform, sug suggest, ass assess,
  el.inf elicit-inform, el.sug elicit-offer-or-suggestion, el.ass elicit-assessment,
  el.und elicit-comment-understanding, off offer, und comment-about-understanding,
  be.pos be-positive, be.neg be-negative, oth other

Absent participants NEVER speak. Speaker labels are ground truth: use only the labels you are given.

The gold annotations must be exactly true of the transcript you write. Refer to segments by their "n" number. Every number you cite must exist.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else: no prose, no markdown fences.

request.user:
Write meeting SY0102d: meeting "d" (detailed design) of series SY0102.

PROJECT
The team is designing a reusable coffee cup with a deposit system.

PARTICIPANTS (label, role, status for this meeting)
A  Marketing Expert (ME)  Sanne  present
B  User Interface designer (UI)  Tomas  ABSENT, never speaks
C  Project Manager (PM)  Rachel  present
D  Industrial Designer (ID)  Martin  present

EARLIER MEETINGS IN THIS SERIES
Stay consistent with them. Refer back to them, follow up on their open action items, and keep the same product and team.

[SY0102a, kickoff]
  abstract: The project manager opened the kickoff meeting and the marketing expert and user interface designer introduced themselves; the industrial designer was absent because of a long-planned supplier visit to a moulding plant in Rotterdam. The project manager introduced the project: a reusable coffee cup with a deposit system for a client chain of about forty coffee shops at train stations and on campuses, aimed at commuters and students, with a production cost under three euros per cup and the client's logo in dark green and white. The team agreed that a lid is essential and must be included within the three-euro cost. The marketing expert identified the deposit amount as the key issue, since too low a deposit discourages returns and too high a deposit discourages uptake. The user interface designer raised a QR code and app or a physical token as ways to prove a deposit was paid, and the marketing expert doubted that commuters want another app. The team decided not to choose materials without the industrial designer's input, and the project manager will send him his tasks after the meeting.
  decisions: The lid is part of the product and must fit within the production cost of under three euros per cup. Material choices will not be made until the industrial designer has given his input. The dishwasher temperature check was moved from the user interface designer to the industrial designer.
  actions: The marketing expert will research deposit amounts and return rates in existing deposit cup schemes. The user interface designer will explore options for the return mechanism, such as a QR code with an app or a token, and present them at the next meeting. The industrial designer will look into materials and durability, including how many uses a cup can last and whether the lid can be made of the same material. The industrial designer will check which dishwasher temperatures the cup must withstand. This task was first given to the user interface designer and then moved to the industrial designer. The project manager will email the industrial designer the slides and action list. The project manager will ask the client whether unreturned cups are a problem for them. The project manager will put the client's corporate colours in the shared folder.
  problems: The deposit amount is still open, pending the marketing expert's research. It is undecided whether returns will use an app with QR codes, a physical token, or another method, and there is concern that commuters will not want another app. It is unclear whether the client minds cups not being returned, given that the café keeps the deposit. The material for the cup and lid is not yet known and depends on the industrial designer's research.
  action item SY0102a.ai1: Research deposit amounts and return rates in existing deposit cup schemes (owner A, active)
  action item SY0102a.ai2: Explore return-mechanism options (QR code and app, token, etc.) and present them at the next meeting (owner B, active)
  action item SY0102a.ai3: Look into cup materials and durability (number of uses), including whether the lid can be the same material (owner D, active)
  action item SY0102a.ai4: Check what dishwasher temperatures the cafés use and the cup must survive (owner D, reassigned)
  action item SY0102a.ai5: Email the absent industrial designer the meeting notes, slides and action list (owner C, active)
  action item SY0102a.ai6: Ask the client whether unreturned cups are a problem for them (owner C, active)
  action item SY0102a.ai7: Put the client's corporate colours in the shared folder (owner C, active)
  fact (absence): The industrial designer (D, Martin) was absent because of a long-planned supplier visit to a moulding plant in Rotterdam.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert's remark about a twenty-euro deposit was a joke and was not adopted.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer suggested a QR code on the cup scanned with an app. The marketing expert doubted that commuters want another app, and no decision was made.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer suggested a physical token such as a plastic coin as proof of deposit. It was left open as one option.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert suggested that unreturned cups might be acceptable because the café keeps the deposit. The project manager will check with the client.
  fact (plan_change): The dishwasher temperature check was first given to the user interface designer and then moved to the industrial designer as a materials question.

[SY0102b, functional design]
  abstract: The project manager opened the functional design meeting, welcomed back the industrial designer, and reported on her actions from the kickoff: she had emailed him the slides and action list, and the client had said that unreturned cups are a problem because it wants to present the cups as a sustainability measure; she had not yet put the corporate colours in the shared folder. The industrial designer presented his materials research, ruling out stainless steel on cost and melamine-bound bamboo fibre on health and heat grounds, and proposed polypropylene for cup and lid at about one euro eighty per cup including the lid, lasting about five hundred uses and withstanding the cafés' dishwasher temperatures of about sixty degrees wash and eighty-five degrees rinse. On the deposit, the marketing expert reported that the largest German scheme charges one euro per cup, that schemes at fifty cents see return rates of about sixty percent and schemes at one euro or more about eighty-five percent, and that returning at any shop helps; the team settled on a deposit of one euro. On returns, the user interface designer compared a QR code with an app, a physical token, and using the cup itself as proof of deposit; given the marketing expert's evidence that apps lower uptake and tokens get lost, the team chose to return the cup itself at the counter of any of the forty shops. The meeting closed with tasks for the conceptual design meeting, including a sample cup, cup markings, a counter sign, competitor research and a comparison of lid types.
  decisions: The cup and lid will both be made of polypropylene. The deposit will be one euro per cup, with the project manager checking with the client about the loss on unreturned cups. Customers return the cup itself at the counter of any of the client's shops to get the deposit back; there will be no app and no token. The counter sign task was moved from the marketing expert to the user interface designer.
  actions: The project manager will put the client's corporate colours in the shared folder today. The project manager will check with the client whether it accepts losing about eighty cents on each cup that is not returned at a one-euro deposit. The industrial designer will ask the Rotterdam plant for a sample cup and a quote for a matte finish. The industrial designer will compare a sip lid and a flip lid, including their costs, for the next meeting. The user interface designer will work out the markings on the cup, including logo placement and how users know the cup can be returned. The user interface designer will design the counter sign explaining the deposit and return; this was first given to the marketing expert and then moved to the user interface designer. The marketing expert will research what competitors' reusable cups look like, including trending colours and shapes.
  problems: Each unreturned cup costs the client about eighty cents more than the one-euro deposit, and it is not yet known whether the client accepts this. Whether to print a QR code on the bottom of the cup so the client can track cups in circulation is left open. There is a concern that a polypropylene cup could look cheap; a matte finish is being considered. The lid type, sip lid or flip lid, has not been chosen.
  action item SY0102b.ai1: Put the client's corporate colours in the shared folder (carried over from the kickoff) (owner C, active)
  action item SY0102b.ai2: Check with the client whether it accepts losing about eighty cents per unreturned cup at a one-euro deposit (owner C, active)
  action item SY0102b.ai3: Get a sample cup from the Rotterdam plant and a quote for a matte finish (owner D, active)
  action item SY0102b.ai4: Work out the markings on the cup: logo placement and how users know they can return it (owner B, active)
  action item SY0102b.ai5: Design the counter sign explaining the deposit and the return (owner B, reassigned)
  action item SY0102b.ai6: Research what competitors' reusable cups look like, including trending colours and shapes (owner A, active)
  action item SY0102b.ai7: Compare a sip lid and a flip lid, including cost, and bring it to the next meeting (owner D, active)
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer suggested printing a QR code on the bottom of the cup so the client can count cups in circulation; the project manager and marketing expert were unconvinced and it was left open.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): Using a QR code on the cup with an app for returns was presented as an option but not adopted, because the marketing expert's research showed apps lower uptake.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): A physical token such as a plastic coin as proof of deposit was presented as an option but not adopted, because customers lose the tokens.
  fact (plan_change): The counter sign task was first given to the marketing expert and then moved to the user interface designer because it is an interface task.

[SY0102c, conceptual design]
  abstract: The project manager opened the conceptual design meeting and reported that the corporate colours were now in the shared folder and that the client accepts losing about eighty cents per unreturned cup, so the one-euro deposit stays; the client will count stock per shop and does not need individual cup tracking, so the team dropped the QR code on the bottom of the cup. The industrial designer showed a standard polypropylene sample from the Rotterdam plant, which the team found light and somewhat cheap-looking, and reported a matte finish at about twelve cents extra and two-colour logo printing at about ten cents; the team chose a matte finish. The marketing expert presented competitor research showing muted, earthy colours and slightly tapered shapes that stack well, and the team agreed on a dark green matte, slightly tapered cup with a white logo in one size. The user interface designer presented the cup markings (white logo on one side, a return message on the other, an embossed one-euro symbol on the base) and a three-step counter sign, which were accepted. On the lid, the industrial designer recommended a sip lid with a slider, rated for the full five hundred washes, and the team adopted it after first leaning towards a flip lid; this brings the cost to about two euros seven per cup, under the three-euro limit.
  decisions: The deposit stays at one euro; the client accepts the loss of about eighty cents on each unreturned cup. No QR code will be printed on the bottom of the cup, since the client will count stock per shop instead of tracking individual cups. The cup will have a matte finish. The cup will be dark green with a white logo and a slightly tapered shape that stacks, in a single size for now. The cup markings are: the white logo on one side about halfway up, the line "Bring me back to any counter, get your euro back" on the other side, and an embossed one-euro symbol on the base. The lid will be a sip lid with a clip-in slider, at about two euros seven per cup in total; this replaces the flip lid the team had first chosen in the meeting.
  actions: The industrial designer will ask the Rotterdam plant for a sample in the client's dark green, matte, with the slider sip lid, using the hex codes from the shared folder. The industrial designer will prepare a full cost breakdown of the final design. The user interface designer will produce the final artwork for the cup markings and the counter sign, trying the wording "any of our forty shops". The marketing expert will put together evaluation criteria for judging the final design at the detailed design meeting. The marketing expert will show the sample cup to a few students at a campus shop to get a quick reaction once the sample is available. The project manager will send the client the concept (dark green matte cup, logo and slider lid) for approval before the design is finalised. The project manager will write the minutes.
  problems: The plant may not be able to match the client's exact dark green. The slider sip lid does not close as tightly as a flip lid, although it does not spill when tipped slightly. Offering two cup sizes was raised and parked; the team stays with one size for now. The client has not yet approved the concept. The counter sign wording ("any shop" or "any of our forty shops") is still to be tried out.
  action item SY0102c.ai1: Check the cost of printing a QR code on the bottom of the cup (owner B, dropped)
  action item SY0102c.ai2: Ask the Rotterdam plant for a sample cup in the client's green, matte, with the slider sip lid (owner D, active)
  action item SY0102c.ai3: Prepare a full cost breakdown of the final design (owner D, active)
  action item SY0102c.ai4: Produce the final artwork for the cup markings and the counter sign, trying the wording "any of our forty shops" (owner B, active)
  action item SY0102c.ai5: Put together evaluation criteria for judging the final design at the detailed design meeting (owner A, active)
  action item SY0102c.ai6: Show the sample cup to a few students at a campus shop to get a quick reaction, once the sample is available (owner A, active)
  action item SY0102c.ai7: Send the client the concept (green matte cup, logo, slider lid) for approval before finalising (owner C, active)
  action item SY0102c.ai8: Write the minutes of the meeting (owner C, active)
  fact (action_item_removed): The user interface designer offered to check the cost of printing a QR code on the bottom of the cup, but the project manager dropped the task because the QR code is no longer needed.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert suggested offering the cup in two sizes; the project manager preferred one size because a second mould is costly, and the idea was parked.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert suggested the counter sign say "any of our forty shops"; the user interface designer agreed only to try it.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer suggested a different lid colour for each shop location; it was rejected because of stock complexity and because cups move between shops.
  fact (plan_change): The team first chose a flip lid but changed to a sip lid with a slider after the industrial designer reported that the flip lid hinge only survives about two hundred washes, against about five hundred for the cup.

EDGE CASES THIS MEETING MUST CONTAIN
Weave each one naturally into the project discussion. Each must be clearly present, and each must be tagged with the segments where it happens.
- F1_ABSENT_DISCUSSED [F1]: One team member is absent. The others discuss them (why they are away, what they would think, what to tell them). The absent person never speaks. The gold summary must not attribute any statement to the absent person.
  Required gold labels: summary, edge_cases.
- F1_SARCASM_AS_FACT [F1]: Someone makes a joke or sarcastic remark phrased as a statement of fact (e.g. "great, so we'll just make it out of solid gold"), and the team does not adopt it. The gold summary must NOT report the joke as a decision or fact.
  Required gold labels: summary, edge_cases.

LENGTH
Between 90 and 140 segments.

GOLD LABELS
- summary: AMI-style abstractive summary in third person, using role names ("The project manager ..."). Sections: abstract (3-6 sentences), actions, decisions, problems (open issues). It reflects the meeting's FINAL state: corrected values, final plans, and no jokes or tangents reported as content.
- action_items: every task arising in the meeting. owner is the speaker label of the FINAL owner, and may be an absent participant. owner is null ONLY for a task nobody takes, with owner_unclear true. status is the final status: active, reassigned (owner changed; previous_owners lists earlier owners) or dropped. history lists the events in order. evidence_segments lists the supporting segments.
- qa_facts: atomic facts someone could later ask about ("Who was asked to ...?", "Did the team agree on ...?"). Include every decision (agreed true), every proposal nobody agreed to (type unagreed_proposal, agreed false), action items, removed action items, absences, and plan changes. Because this meeting follows earlier ones, include at least one fact of type reference_to_prior_meeting, with refers_to_meeting set, at a point where someone refers back to an earlier meeting. Do NOT write questions.
- edge_cases: one entry per edge case above, with its scenario_id and the segment numbers that contain it.

OUTPUT JSON SHAPE
{
  "segments": [{"n": 1, "speaker": "A", "da_type": "inf", "text": "..."}],
  "summary": {"abstract": ["..."], "actions": ["..."], "decisions": ["..."], "problems": ["..."]},
  "action_items": [{"n": 1, "description": "...", "owner": "C", "owner_unclear": false, "status": "active", "previous_owners": [], "history": [{"segment": 12, "event": "assigned", "by": "A", "owner": "C"}], "evidence_segments": [12, 13]}],
  "qa_facts": [{"type": "decision", "fact": "...", "agreed": true, "related_action_item": null, "refers_to_meeting": null, "evidence_segments": [40]}],
  "edge_cases": [{"scenario_id": "...", "segments": [20, 21, 22], "note": "one line on how it appears"}]
}
history events: proposed, offered, assigned, accepted, reassigned, dropped, restated. qa_facts types: decision, unagreed_proposal, action_item, action_item_removed, absence, plan_change, reference_to_prior_meeting, other. related_action_item is an action item's "n" or null. refers_to_meeting is an earlier meeting ID of this series or null.
